content: Nutritional labelling is promoted as a strategy to encourage healthier food and beverage choices, including reducing overall energy intake. Various nutritional labelling systems have been implemented globally, but there is no clear agreement on their effectiveness in fostering healthier behaviors. The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the impact of nutritional labelling on the purchasing and consumption of healthier food and non-alcoholic drink options. A secondary objective was to investigate factors that might influence the effectiveness of nutritional labelling. To achieve this, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of 13 electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to April 26, 2017. They also manually reviewed references and citations and sought unpublished studies through online platforms and trial registries. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized controlled trials (Q-RCTs), controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series (ITS) studies. These studies compared products with nutritional labels (e.g., nutrient or energy information) to the same products without labels and measured purchasing or consumption in real-world or laboratory settings. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion and extracted data. The quality of evidence was assessed using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool and the GRADE framework. Where possible, data from similar studies were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, while other findings were summarized narratively. A total of 28 studies were included in the review, comprising 17 RCTs, 5 Q-RCTs, and 6 ITS studies. Most studies (21 out of 28) were conducted in the United States, with 19 taking place in university settings, often involving students or staff. Twenty studies examined the effects of nutritional labelling on menus, menu boards, or adjacent to food and drink options, while eight studies focused on single labelled food or drink items. The most commonly assessed type of labelling was energy (calorie) information, evaluated in 12 studies. Eleven studies investigated the impact of nutritional labelling on food and drink purchases in real-world settings, such as vending machines, grocery stores, restaurants, cafeterias, or coffee shops. However, findings from vending machine and grocery store studies were inconclusive and rated as very low quality. A meta-analysis of three RCTs assessing energy labelling on restaurant menus showed a statistically significant reduction of 47 kcal in energy purchased per meal (mean difference: −46.72 kcal, 95% confidence interval: −78.35 to −15.10, N = 1877). This corresponds to a 7.8% reduction in energy purchased per meal, assuming an average meal contains 600 kcal. However, the quality of evidence was rated as low, indicating limited confidence in the findings, which may change with further research. Two additional ITS studies with low risk of bias supported these results, while four other studies had unclear reporting and high risk of bias. Seventeen studies assessed the impact of nutritional labelling on food consumption in laboratory settings. Eight of these studies (all RCTs) evaluated the effect of labelling on menus or a range of food options. A meta-analysis of these studies did not show a conclusive reduction in energy consumed during a meal (mean difference: −50 kcal, 95% confidence interval: −104.41 to 3.88, N = 1705). The quality of evidence was rated as low, suggesting limited confidence in the findings. Six laboratory studies (four RCTs and two Q-RCTs) examined the impact of labelling a single food or drink item (e.g., chocolate, pasta, or soft drinks) on energy consumed during a snack or meal. A meta-analysis of these studies found no statistically significant difference in energy consumed (standardized mean difference: 0.05, 95% confidence interval: −0.17 to 0.27, N = 732). The wide confidence intervals indicate uncertainty in the true effect size, and the quality of evidence was rated as low. There was no evidence to suggest that nutritional labelling caused unintended harm, such as increasing energy purchased or consumed. Five laboratory studies investigated the effects of mislabelling (e.g., labelling high-energy foods as low-energy or low-fat) on energy consumption during a snack or meal. A meta-analysis of these studies found no statistically significant increase in energy consumed (standardized mean difference: 0.19, 95% confidence interval: −0.14 to 0.51, N = 718). The effect size was small, and the wide confidence intervals suggest uncertainty. The quality of evidence from these studies was rated as very low, providing minimal confidence in the findings. In conclusion, findings from a limited body of low-quality evidence suggest that energy labelling on menus may reduce energy purchased in restaurant settings. Evidence on the impact of energy labelling on consumption in laboratory settings indicates a similar trend but is less definitive and also of low quality. Given the absence of observed harms, nutritional labelling on menus in restaurants could be considered as part of a broader strategy to address obesity. However, additional high-quality research in real-world settings is needed to draw more definitive conclusions. Further studies are also required to address the lack of evidence from grocery stores and vending machines and to explore potential factors that may influence the effectiveness of nutritional labelling, such as socioeconomic status.
